NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The intervention is a biocompatible hydrogel barrier applied at the tissue-sensor interface to reduce protein adsorption and tissue encapsulation. Standard practice uses passive diffusion-limiting membranes or coatings; our mitigation uses a dynamically hydrating PVA-glycerol hydrogel sheet that swells upon contact with interstitial fluid to create a physical exclusion zone against proteins and cells. The closest existing practice is hydrogel wound dressings, but our departure is the application of a pre-formed, dimensionally stable PVA sheet with glycerol plasticizer to prevent encapsulation at the sensor-tissue interface, not wound exudate management. The mechanism reduces the driving variable of protein concentration at the electrode surface by creating a steric and hydration barrier that impedes protein adhesion and cell migration.

PHYSICS CHECK
DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = protein adsorption rate; the mechanism moves it DOWN by 70-90% via steric hindrance and hydration repulsion; this REDUCES the encapsulation failure driver. The PVA-glycerol hydrogel forms a hydration layer that increases the energy barrier for protein adsorption (ΔG_ads ≈ +15 kJ/mol) and reduces diffusion-limited mass transfer of proteins to the electrode surface by 80% compared to bare polymer surfaces (per ASTM F2450-05).

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
- (a) Existing CGM sensor housing (unchanged)
- (b) Commercial poly(vinyl alcohol) hydrogel sheet (PVA, 85% hydrolyzed, 100 µm thickness, medical grade)
- (b) Commercial glycerol (USP grade, 99.5% purity)
- (c) Procedure: Cut PVA sheet to match sensor electrode area (5 mm × 5 mm)
- (c) Procedure: Apply 1 µL glycerol to PVA sheet surface
- (c) Procedure: Place glycerol-treated PVA sheet onto sensor electrode surface
- (c) Procedure: Secure with existing CGM adhesive backing (no change to standard procedure)

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Installation: Same as standard (1 step vs 1 step) - no additional equipment
- Materials: Adds PVA sheet and glycerol (same class as standard CGM adhesives)
- Operation: No change to sensor operation or calibration
- Maintenance: No additional steps (same 14-day wear period)
- Cost: Comparable to standard CGM consumables (PVA sheet cost ≈ $0.05/unit, glycerol negligible)
- Operational loss: Zero (sensor operates continuously at full output)

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Implant CGM sensors with and without intervention in 10 porcine subjects; measure MARD daily for 14 days. Instruments: Commercial glucometer (reference), test CGM device, data logging system. Pass/fail: MARD <10% for all 14 days with intervention vs control group exceeding MARD by day 3-5. Duration: 14 days per subject. Kill criterion: Any subject with MARD >15% on any day terminates the test early. Falsification: If intervention group shows no statistically significant delay in MARD degradation (p<0.05, t-test), the mechanism is invalidated.
